ai.text:
The European Commission has proposed a regulation that aims to cut red tape for businesses in the EU's single market while still protecting consumers and the environment. The proposal changes several existing EU product rules, covering areas such as cableway installations, personal protective equipment, gas-burning appliances, machinery, batteries, and ecodesign for sustainable products. Its main goal is to replace paper-based paperwork with digital versions, so companies can submit and share information more easily and national authorities can check compliance more efficiently.

Under the proposal, the EU declaration of conformity, or a similar document, must be made electronically and be accessible through an internet address or machine-readable code when it needs to go with a product. Manufacturers would also have to list a "digital contact" on products placed on the market to make it easier for businesses and national authorities to communicate. Once the European Business Wallet is available, the digital address it provides could serve as this digital contact.

Product instructions could be provided electronically, except for safety information, which must still be given on paper or marked on the product for consumers. Reporting obligations to national authorities that currently allow a "paper or electronic format" would be changed to require electronic form only. The proposal also requires electronic exchanges between economic operators and competent authorities, and it introduces common specifications as an alternative to harmonised standards.

Finally, where a product is covered by other EU legislation that requires a digital product passport, the information in the EU declaration of conformity and instructions must also be provided through that passport. The proposal is part of the Commission's fourth simplification package and is to be adopted by the European Parliament and the Council under the ordinary legislative procedure, on an equal footing.
